outcome.description: You fall into formation with the convoy and maintain a watchful sensor sweep. The transit passes without incident, though your presence likely deterred at least one contact that appeared on long-range scans and then vanished. Associate Director Novik transfers your fee with a formal note of thanks from Solari Logistics.

Novik hesitates, then consults with his logistics team. "Solari Logistics is authorized to increase the offer by forty percent, given the elevated threat assessment. Do we have an agreement?" You accept, and the convoy proceeds under your watchful eye.

Novik accepts your refusal with the composure of a man accustomed to logistics setbacks. "Understood. Safe travels, Captain." The convoy tightens formation and continues on, their running lights blinking nervously in the dark.

You dock with the Golden Dividend and help their engineer jury-rig the heating array with components from your own ship. Within an hour, the galley is operational again. The executives applaud as the first hot meal in six hours emerges from the kitchen. The purser pays you with the desperate generosity of a person whose job was on the line.

You heat up your entire stock of emergency ration packs and shuttle them over. The executives eye the bland nutrient bars with undisguised horror, but hunger wins. The purser pays you triple the going rate and thanks you through gritted teeth. "The passengers have been... adequately sustained."

You log the distress signal, note that no lives are in danger, and continue on your route. Behind you, the Golden Dividend's purser can be heard arguing with an executive who is demanding to speak with "whoever is in charge of the universe's logistics."

You dock up and Fen's crew slings crates across with practiced ease. 'My grandmother used to say a full hold and an empty tank still beats the other way round,' Fen laughs. He insists you keep a few crates for the trouble.

It takes careful flying, but between your thrusters and his, the hauler straightens out. Fen transmits a thank-you along with some Verdant Cooperative trade vouchers. 'Tell 'em Fen sent you. They'll treat you right.'
Fen nods without judgment. 'Fair enough, friend. Fly safe.' His hauler groans onward, listing but stubborn. Frontier folk manage.

You pull alongside and your toolkit does the rest . A cracked coolant line and a burned relay. Two hours of sweaty work in Nabil's engine bay, but the unit hums back to life. 'You just saved a season's worth of food,' Nabil says, voice thick. 'The cooperative will hear about this. That's a promise, not a proverb.'

You split the flashfruit between both ships. Your hold can keep it cool enough. Half a harvest saved is better than none, and Nabil insists you sell your share. 'It's honest pay for honest help. That's how we do things.'
Nabil's voice fades behind you, still calling on the open channel. Somewhere, three stations will have a lean month. The frontier remembers who showed up and who kept flying.
You transmit emergency treatment protocols and dock briefly to transfer supplies. The freighter captain thanks you profusely and insists on paying for the help.
You log the distress coordinates for the next patrol and continue on your route. The signal fades behind you.
The tow takes time and fuel, but the pilot's relief is palpable. They transfer payment the moment you reach the station.
You amplify their signal to reach local patrols. It's the best you can do without losing time. Hopefully help arrives in time.
The pilot accepts your data with minimal embarrassment. A grateful passenger sends you a small tip through the ship's comm channel.
You leave them to sort out their own heading. Space is big, but the lanes are well-charted. They'll manage.

You pull alongside the Heron and patch your fuel line into their auxiliary systems. Captain Sato's voice comes through, steady but exhausted: 'I owe you one, Captain. The raiders took everything . Cargo, navigation data, even the crew manifests. This wasn't random. They knew exactly where we'd be.' She transfers a small credit bounty from the escort's emergency fund.
You silence the distress channel and continue on course. The signal fades behind you. Somewhere out there, Captain Sato is counting the hours on her life support.
You hard-dock and cycle fresh atmosphere into the prospector's cabin. Color returns to her face as she gulps clean air. She insists on transferring her claim credits .'Won't need them if I'm dead.'
You pump power into their beacon until it lights up every receiver in the sector. A mining barge responds within minutes. You move on, hoping two hours was a conservative estimate.

You burn hard toward the firefight, weapons hot. The raiders see you coming and break off . Two against two isn't the odds they wanted. The freighter captain nearly weeps with relief and transfers every credit she can spare.

You light up every patrol channel in range with the freighter's coordinates. A Guild corvette responds within minutes, but by the time it arrives, the raiders have stripped the freighter and fled. At least the crew survived.
You alter course and give the battle a wide berth. The weapons fire fades from your sensors. You tell yourself there was nothing you could have done. It almost sounds convincing.

You find debris. Not much . A sheared hull panel, frozen coolant, a cargo manifest floating in the void. The ship's name was the Perihelion. Crew of four. Nobody's coming for them anymore. You log the coordinates and move on.
You flag the beacon in the sector registry. Somewhere, an office will update a file. Somewhere else, a family is still waiting for a ship that isn't coming back.

The Sundog is venting atmosphere from a dozen hull breaches. Not pirates . The damage pattern is internal. Stress fractures in the alloy composite. Cheap materials, corners cut. The captain's last log names the manufacturer and the contract that approved the hull grade. You copy everything.
You cut the channel and adjust course. The signal fades. Whatever happened to the Sundog, it'll happen to someone else eventually. That's how corners get cut.

'Appreciate it, but we've got it handled,' the hauler captain replies. 'Name's Maren. We run this lane twice a week . You see enough breakdowns, you keep a tow rig handy.' You're not the only one out here who stops. Good to remember.
You watch the hauler guide the shuttle toward the nearest station and resume your route. One less problem in the lane. Someone else's good deed.

The docking clamp locks onto the pod with a shudder that travels through your whole hull. Inside, a woman in a torn flight suit is barely conscious. Her first words are coordinates, repeated like a prayer. She's been drifting for three days. You set course for the nearest station.

You crack the pod's hatch. The survivor inside is dehydrated and incoherent but alive. You pull her out, strip the pod's intact hull plating and fuel cell, and set course for the nearest station. She'll recover. The pod won't.
You log the coordinates and transmit them on the emergency frequency. The pod shrinks in your rear sensors until it's just another point of light. The patrol frequency doesn't acknowledge.

You reel in the carrier. The cat . A massive orange tabby . Stares at you through the mesh with the cold fury of a creature that has seen the void and found it personally offensive. A tag on the carrier reads 'PROPERTY OF DR. VASQUEZ, BREAKSTONE STATION. IF FOUND, KEEP HIM. I'M DONE.' The cat immediately claims your pilot seat. You find a reward notice on the station boards later . Apparently Dr. Vasquez changed her mind.

Three people respond. None of them are missing a cat . They all want one. A bidding war breaks out on open comms. You broker the adoption to a lonely ice miner who promises to name the cat 'Admiral.' The miner sends you a finder's fee, and the cat seems to approve of someone who lives in a place as cold and inhospitable as space.
You leave the carrier tumbling through space. The cat watches your ship recede with an expression that suggests it will remember this. Somehow, you believe it.

You dock at the shaft's emergency port and offload everything you can spare. Tomek grips your hand hard enough to bruise. 'We don't forget this. None of us do.' Twelve hours later, all seventeen come up alive. The co-op wires you compensation from the emergency fund.
You patch their signal through your long-range array. Union rescue ships respond within the hour. Tomek's voice comes back on comms: 'Appreciate it, friend. Every minute counts down here.'
You log the coordinates and keep flying. The signal fades behind you, but Tomek's voice stays in your head longer than you'd like.

You tow Harlan's rig to a safe orbit and patch his coolant line with sealant tape. He's sheepish about the whole thing. Jess's voice crackles over comms: 'Well, at least someone's got a conscience. Tell Harlan his invoice is in the mail.' Both sides grudgingly respect the call.

Jess goes quiet for a long moment. Then: 'Yeah, alright. You're right and I hate it.' The Union crew moves in to help. Later, Harlan quietly asks Jess about membership rates. She pretends not to smile.
You fly on, leaving the bickering behind. As you pull away, you hear Jess sigh and say, 'Fine. Warm up the tow line.' Some things work themselves out.

Threading through the rocks takes nerve, but you find Nils in a one-person prospector pod, running on fumes. He's gaunt but grinning when you dock. 'Three days on protein paste and bad air. Could've been worse . Could've been four.' He insists on splitting his last ore haul with you. Union prospectors pay their debts.

You boost his beacon and tag the coordinates for Union search-and-rescue. A dispatcher confirms they're scrambling a recovery team. Nils's voice comes back, quieter: 'Appreciate it. Tell 'em to bring coffee, yeah?'
You tag the signal in your nav log and continue on course. Nils doesn't say anything else. The beacon keeps pulsing, small and steady, swallowed by the vastness of the field.

You match speed with Mercy-Seven and run interference through the corridor. Your presence deters two contacts that were shadowing the transport. Dr. Adeyemi exhales audibly as you clear the danger zone: 'Four patients will receive transplants today because of your decision, Captain. The Okafor Institute is transferring an escort stipend, but the debt is larger than credits can express.'

You accompany Mercy-Seven through the worst stretch before peeling off at the junction. Dr. Adeyemi thanks you: 'Even partial coverage improves our survival probability by an estimated 60 percent. Every kilometer counts.' A partial stipend arrives.

Dr. Adeyemi accepts without recrimination. 'Understood, Captain. We will increase speed and hope the corridor is clear. Mercy-Seven out.' The transport accelerates past you, running dark, organ units humming in the hold.

Following Holm's precise instructions, you maneuver alongside the buoy and transmit the shutdown code sequence. The buoy's power cell goes dormant, radiation levels dropping immediately. Holm's relief is audible despite the clinical delivery: 'Shutdown confirmed. Radiation output now at background levels. You have potentially prevented acute exposure for dozens of transiting vessels. Hazard mitigation payment authorized. Thank you, Captain.'

You amplify the buoy's warning signal and add your own transponder data to mark the hazard zone. Holm acknowledges: 'A practical interim measure. It will not eliminate the exposure risk, but informed avoidance is the next best outcome. We have noted your assistance.'

You plot a course well around the leaking buoy. Holm sighs: 'Noted. The recovery team will arrive when they arrive. In the meantime, the corridor remains hazardous.' The automated warning continues its monotone broadcast.

You walk the tourists through resetting their autopilot, which takes longer than it should because Reginald keeps pressing the wrong buttons. Eventually the yacht lurches onto the correct heading. The grateful passenger transfers a generous tip. "You're a lifesaver, Captain! Much better service than the concierge, honestly."

You spend half an hour babysitting the yacht back to Stellaris Port's tourist ring. The passengers treat it like an adventure, taking holographs of your ship from every angle. The port authority logs your assist and the tourists insist on paying for your docking fees plus a 'hazard bonus' . Their words.
You leave the yacht to its slow, confused orbit. Port Authority will pick them up eventually. Reginald is still pressing buttons as you fly away.

You navigate through venting gas and debris to reach the Delta Wing emergency lock. The workers . Soot-covered, shaken, but alive . Crowd into your cargo bay. The last one out, a shift foreman named Brennan, grips your hand hard enough to hurt. Crucible Station transfers an emergency services bounty to your account.

You pump power into your comms array and rebroadcast the distress call on every frequency. Two mining haulers with heavy shielding respond within minutes and head for the station. You did your part . Sometimes the best help is getting the right people there faster.
You pull back to a safe perimeter and watch the emergency unfold from a distance. Rescue shuttles eventually reach Delta Wing. The workers make it out, but it takes longer than it should have.

Your sensors penetrate the rubble and detect life signs . Faint but present. You relay the scan data to the nearest Union rescue team, cutting their search time in half. The rescue coordinator, a gruff woman named Kowalski, patches through when the miners are pulled out alive: "Your scans saved three people today, Captain. Union doesn't forget that."

You amplify the distress beacon and broadcast it on Union priority channels. A rescue team acknowledges within minutes. You've done what you can from out here . The rest is on the people with the drilling equipment and the nerve to go underground.
You log the beacon coordinates and continue on your route. Shaft collapses happen in Breakstone . The Union has teams for this. You tell yourself that, anyway.
